seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

msIdentifier.repository: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library, Yale University

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p:
Dear Pound: I sent you a card yesterday, interrupted I fear. My eyes are quiet for the moment – probably because I have been ill for the past week with my throat – the intention of providence being perhaps to take away my voice and thus leave me without even that to fall back on. (The prima donna
of the opera here heard me a few days ago singing. She lives at the end of this house. She stopped my wife in the corridor and said I had a wunderschöne Stimme and asked would I go with her on tour for concerts during the operatic recess.) Perhaps it is this climate which brings to the surface and magnifies every weakness of the body or perhaps it is the result of nine years’ worry breaking out here and there. I make a special diet, without fish, meat, fowl, tea, coffee, cocoa, chocolate, eggs, lentils, peas, beans, composed chiefly of oatmeal and various leaves. Needless to say I do not mind this in the least and would exist cheerfully on sawdust if I could avoid an operation thereby. Dr Gould ’s opinion evidently is to operate all cases of glaucoma. There is something to be said for doctors because they do not know much and want to prevent any possibility of disaster. I am (or was) making a treatment for the blood and shall resume it again in September when the next instalment of money arrives as it is rather expensive.

I am quite tired in consequence of a very long letter which my agent made me write. Mr Richards announced his intention of publishing Exiles on the basis of my agreement with him for Dubliners . My agent asked why I signed such a contract. In my reply I told him why. My wife had a letter today from Mr Quinn who has received the first act of Exiles in MS. I shall await the arrival of his next letter in which he will probably acknowledge receipt of the other acts. He says he would like to have a copy of the typescript sent on as he fears it could not be typed from my MS without risk of mistakes. If you are writing him meanwhile please say that the MS is his property but he can give it or lend it to Mr Huebsch to set from direct. The MS is quite legible, I think. If Mr Huebsch has not a right of refusal over this play by contract he is, in my view, entitled to such a right by courtesy. Mr Huebsch can publish this play as soon as he likes and, so far as I am concerned, make a contract for it afterwards. I want it to be published as I wrote it and out of my way. As for production I know nothing. As I told you it was refused here, in Turin and in Berne. The Stage Society kept it for several months, sent it back. Then the Abbey Theatre Company wrote for it, seemingly in a great hurry, kept it several months, sent it back. Then the Stage Society wrote for it again and kept it several months more so that I have now instructed my agent to withdraw it by telephone and to offer it to nobody else unless the person receiving it undertakes to give his opinion within three weeks. My daughter (who knows no English) could spell her way through it in that time and I assume that a publisher or an impresario can do the same. If they cannot I shall not allow them to waste my time as they have done till now.

I am looking forward to reading your poem . I am sure it will be
scintillante di giovinezza
and I hope you put in one or two sweet lines for my oldfashioned ear. I asked you in my card if you could print music in your review because there is a friend of mine here, a Spaniard , who has read some of your verses and perhaps he would send some pages for your review. He has set some by Albert Samain – La Ville Morte. I hear there is a Russian notice of my novel. There will be one also in a London Greek journal –
Η
ΕΣΠΕRΙΑ ΕΣΠΕΡΙΑ
. Miss Weaver is trying to get a notice at my suggestion in some Italian paper. Meanwhile the sales are 1 per 100,000 of the population.
I nunc et tecum
… .

closer.salute: With friendliest regards to Mrs Pound & yourself

div.note: JJ’s postcard to Pound of 7 July 1917 (but postmarked “yesterday,” 8 July 1917), which he anxiously broke off at the approach of a thunderstorm.
JJ wrote Harriet Shaw Weaver on 7 July 1917: “I have been laid up for the past week with fever and tonsillitis. I am better today” (LI 103).

Charlotte Sauermann (1880-1931), a soprano with the Zurich opera, occupied rooms next to those rented by JJ and his family at Seefeldstrasse 73. She admired JJ’s singing voice and wanted to help him find work at the Zurich opera house, but he declined. In 1918, Sauermann was the one to reveal to JJ the identity of the person — Mrs. Harold McCormick — who had made him an anonymous gift of 1,000 francs per month beginning March 1918 (Ellmann, JJ 422). Philipp Jarnach (1892-1982), composer and secretary to the composer Ferruccio Busoni (1866-1924), also occupied rooms at Seefeldstrasse 73, and it is possible that he and Sauermann were living together (Carol Loeb Shloss, Lucia Joyce: To Dance in the Wake [New York: Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 2003], 71). Sauermann, sometimes billed as Lotte or with her married name Ofner or Sauermann-Ofner, excelled as a concert singer. For example, she sang Schumann lieder and selections from Weber’s opera Oberon in Aarau, Switzerland, in November 1917; performed in Beethoven’s Missa solemnis in Neuchâtel in April 1921, and in Verdi’s Requiem in Vienna in November 1925; and sang Mahler lieder in Vienna in January 1926. JJ later helped her son to escape from Nazi territory (Ellmann, JJ 709).
Ger. “very beautiful voice.”

George Milbry Gould (1848-1922), noted American ophthalmologist and prolific author. Pound had been treated by Gould some years before this, and felt that he might be able to help JJ. For a full account, see JJ to Pound, 13 April 1917, notes.

JJ learned in February 1917 from London solicitors that an anonymous “admirer of [his] writing” had gifted him £200, to be paid in £50 installments in May, August, November, and the next February (LII 389). JJ thought that Pound was involved, but the admirer was later revealed to be Harriet Shaw Weaver.
In reply to a letter of 2 July 1917 from his London literary agent J.B. Pinker, JJ wrote a long and exasperated letter on 8 July 1917 (LII 398-400). See JJ to Pound, 7 July 1917, notes.
Quinn’s cablegram to Pound dated 15 August 1917 confirmed that he had received acts two and three of the Exiles manuscript (Pound/Joyce 123).

JJ wrote Quinn on 10 July 1917 to suggest that if he did not wish to allow the American printers to work from the Exiles manuscript, “it can be typed first – charge of typing being to my account.” JJ added that he would have the corrected “English printed proofs” sent on later to New York to “serve as a control” (LI 104).
Both B.W. Huebsch in New York and Grant Richards in London published Exiles in May 1918.

Although W.B. Yeats (1865-1939), enthusiastic after reading A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man, initially thought the Dublin Abbey Theatre might stage Exiles, he later wrote JJ that “it is a type of work we have never played well” since it was “too far from the folk drama.” He thought it “[not] at all so good” as A Portrait (quoted in Ellmann, JJ 401-02).

The London Incorporated Stage Society considered Exiles during 1916 and 1917 but in the end did not stage it (see JJ to Pound, 5 June 1917, notes). JJ became exasperated with delays and wrote his London agent J.B. Pinker on 8 July 1917 to get the typescript back from the Society (LII 398).
JJ and his family often spoke Triestine Italian at home.
Pound’s “Three Cantos.” See JJ to Pound, 30 March 1917, notes, and 7 July 1917, notes.
It. “sparkling with youth.”

In his letter of 17 July 1917, Pound granted JJ’s request for “one or two sweet lines for my oldfashioned ear” by offering some “mellifluous archaism” in the form of a dozen lines “mistranslating Horace” (Pound/Joyce 122-23).

Philipp Jarnach (1892-1982), born in France, was the son of a Spanish sculptor. In Zurich during World War I, Jarnach was a student of and secretary to the composer Ferruccio Busoni (1866-1924), and was himself a composer and later a teacher of composition. JJ and his family rented rooms next to those occupied by Jarnach at Seefeldstrasse 73. See JJ to Pound, 19 March 1917, notes.

Albert Samain (1858-1900) was a French Symbolist poet, strongly influenced by Charles Baudelaire and Paul Verlaine. His sonnet “Ville morte” tells of a once great Eastern city, “empty now and forever silent” (“[v]ide à present, et pour jaimais silencieuse”), in the midst of whose ruins a great bronze elephant tragically lifts its trunk to the stars. Around 1911, Philipp Jarnach set Samain’s poems, “Ville morte” and “Arpège,” for piano and voice. JJ was interested enough in Samain to copy “Arpège” and several of his other poems, along with additional French verse, into a notebook he compiled in 1919-1920 in Trieste (Peter Spielberg, James Joyce’s Manuscripts and Letters at the University of Buffalo: A Catalogue [Buffalo, NY: University of Buffalo, 1962], 168-69).

The Hesperia: A Greek Weekly Illustrated Newspaper, launched in London in 1916 under the editorship of Dr. Constantine Pouptis (1878-1942), was devoted to enhancing understanding of Greek national questions and the development of Greek literature, art, and commerce. JJ told Weaver that a notice of A Portrait appeared in the journal for 29 June 1917, page 410 (LI 107).

Probably an allusion to Horace, Epistle 2. 2. 76, “I nunc, et versus tecum meditare canoros” (“Now go and meditate on melodious verses”), an ironic glance at the plight of the contemplative poet distracted by the noise and bustle of the Roman streets. JJ suggests he is similarly harried by circumstances. This allusion may have stimulated Pound to include twelve lines “mistranslating Horace” in his letter to JJ of 17 July 1917 (Pound/Joyce 122-23).
